newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Beijing official says entry to H.K. being blocked.
newsitem.headline: Beijing official says entry to H.K. being blocked.

text.p: China sent out a sour New Year's Eve signal with Beijing's top official on Hong Kong accusing Britain of blocking his entry into the colony before its return to China in mid-1997.

Lu Ping, head of Beijing's Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, said in a television interview from Beijing that he had received a visa to enter Hong Kong which was valid until December 15 and had been unable to come to the British territory since then.
Lu said the problem was one reason a meeting of the committee which elected Hong Kong's post-colonial legislature was held in China on December 21 instead of in Hong Kong.
"You go to Hong Kong to hold an election, but the British don't agree ... and refuse to cooperate," Lu told Hong Kong's ATV television Chinese-language news programme on Tuesday.

"Why did they give this visa only until December 15? Obviously, because of that. Because on December 21 the provisional legislature was being elected. So they would not allow me to go Hong Kong, would they?"

A spokesman for Governor Chris Patten told Reuters it was not the government's practice to comment on individual visa cases, but he expressed bewilderment that Lu had lumped himself together with the 400 members of the Selection Committee.

"I'm a bit puzzled by him saying he couldn't come for a meeting of the Selection Committee. He's not even a member of the Selection Committee. All the members of the committee are people of Hong Kong, and they don't need visas to be here," the spokesman said.

"If he had felt strongly enough about wanting to come to Hong Kong again to hold the Selection Committee meeting for the provisional legislature in the territory, then I'm sure the arrangements could have been made for him."

Patten says he will not cooperate with the provisional legislature, to be installed after midnight next June 30 when the British pull out, because it runs foul of the treaty under which Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty.
Sino-British relations have suffered jolts over the handover but this is the first accusation about visa problems levelled against the colonial authorities by China.
"They won't even give me a visa, how can I meet him?" Lu Ping said when asked if he would meet Patten before the territory reverts to China.
Patten and Lu have not been on speaking terms since the Governor introduced electoral reforms in the colony.
Hong Kong's post-colonial successor, Tung Chee-hwa, said on Monday the caretaker chamber would soon hold its first meeting, but it would be in China, not Hong Kong.
"The provisional legislature must meet for the first time. It'll probably be in Shenzhen. It would be very soon," Tung said.

The provisional legislature is staunchly opposed by Hong Kong's Democratic Party. The party emerged from 1995 elections for the present Legislative Council with the most votes of any party, but will lose its seats upon the handover.
The party says the interim legislature will be illegal if it functions before the change of flag, and their threats of legal action have forced the body to meet in China.
